Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy.
Huang, who heads a leading AI chipmaker and is an ally of President Donald Trump , apologized in a message to the company, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife” and took "full responsibility" for his actions.
“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
The company said that while its board had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry would examine all available information.
It said that the board has confidence in Huang and his ⁠leadership team, adding that the CEO fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.
Late last month, the New York Times reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center.
Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.
When asked about Alice Huang being suspected of spying for China, Liu Chang, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, told the Times the U.S. was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against the Asian country.
Trump said on Sunday he had not spoken to Huang about ​the allegations, but ⁠called him a fine person.
"I hope everything's fine. He's done such an ‌incredible job," he added.
When asked if he believed he should have acted on intelligence when he was briefed about it, Trump said: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it."
Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips. It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
However, the investigation adds to pressure on Nvidia at a time investors are already pulling back amid uncertainty over the sustainability of the booming AI market.
Nvidia shares fell in out-of-hours trading on Monday and extended to South Korea, where Madison Huang, Huang's daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled a planned visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference set to begin this week.
But Seoul expects contracted deliveries of Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) to proceed without disruption despite a controversy surrounding Huang. Vice Minister of Science and ICT Ryu Jemyung told a parliamentary budget committee that 10,000 GPUs funded under a 2025 supplementary budget had already arrived and were in use.
Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told the Times on Sunday that “today’s news will not slow Nvidia”. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.”
Huang, like other tech leaders, has flocked to Trump as the president embraces AI. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. His attendance wasn’t unusual, given that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg were also there.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to say whether Huang was excluded from U.S. briefings in light of the recent reporting. He told reporters Sunday before departing for France, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it.”
Trump is a major backer of AI, trying to rebrand the technology as SI for “Super Intelligence” and loosen regulations.
While Huang may be an ally to the president, it will be hard to overlook a potential security breach from not only a U.S. adversary, but also its top competitor in the AI race.
“We’re leading China in AI,” the president said in September amid concerns that AI could pose an existential threat to humans . “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
Billionaire investor Bill Ackman said on X that the Nvidia CEO was an "incredible human," but if "indeed this is more ⁠than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem."
"I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security," he added.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk commented "I agree" on a post by Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that said Huang "did something incredibly dumb" that was "bad for America" but that "Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership".
The Independent has reached out to the State Department and the White House for comment.

articles.title_zh: Dow surges 1,100 points, Nasdaq climbs more than 2% as tech rebounds from last week’s tumult: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks surged on Monday, boosted by a decline in oil prices as well as gains in technology shares after last week's volatility.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average popped 1,104.02 points, or 2.15%, to close at 52,389.75. The blue-chip index was supported by gains in stocks such as Goldman Sachs and Caterpillar . The S&P 500 rose 2.35% to end at 7,549.94 for its best day since April 8, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 2.74% to 25,253.14.
With Monday's rally, the Dow is now above the level it closed on Election Day. The S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq still remain slightly below, however.
Oil prices fell on Monday, lifting investor sentiment. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures dropped 4.38% to settle at $86.85 per barrel. International benchmark Brent slid 5.85% to $92.57 per barrel.
Friday's market partially rebounded from Thursday's brutal artificial intelligence-driven sell-off, as chip stocks recovered on renewed buying. However, concerns linger in the wake of the Democrats' strong midterm results, with investors fearing that tighter regulations on data center construction, energy use, and development costs could slow the AI infrastructure boom .
The tech sector also focused on the bombshell announcement Sunday that Nvidia's board of directors is opening an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares closed down 4%.
"Magnificent Seven" names were higher contrary to Nvidia. Amazon gained about 3%, while Tesla and Alphabet climbed 5.5% and 1%, respectively. Microsoft also added almost 3%.
Other chip stocks advanced as well, with Broadcom popping nearly 9% and Advanced Micro Devices jumping 13%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) — which dropped around 13% last week — rose more than 7%.
The recent chip sell-off was "overdone," said Jay Hatfield, CEO at Infrastructure Capital Advisors. The turmoil was still "partially correct," he added, given that there "definitely is a policy overhang from the Democrats in both the short run, but, more importantly, in the long run from '28." To be sure, he believes data centers are ultimately "going to get built" in the U.S.
For the broader market, Hatfield said that "it's not like the coast is clear" with Monday's bounce. In fact, he anticipates the S&P 500 will be rangebound through the end of the year.
"There are still a lot of overhangs on the market," the CEO said, pointing to elevated oil prices as a result of the Middle East conflict as well as the Federal Reserve's interest rate outlook.
This week , investors are looking ahead to key AI-related earnings — CoreWeave , Cisco and Applied Materials are all on deck — as they assess the outlook for tech and whether the recent sell-off has further to run.
They'll also watch for the releases of both the consumer price index on Tuesday and the producer price index on Friday, looking for clues on the Fed's next move.
The three U.S. leading indexes popped on Monday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1,104.02, or 2.15%, to settle at 52,389.75. The S&P 500 rose 2.35% to close at 7,549.94, while the Nasdaq Composite jumped 2.74% to 25,253.14.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) surged more than 8% to start the week amid a revival in tech shares.
Monday's advance in SOXX puts it on course for its best day since July 30.
Monolithic Power , a maker of power modules, and semiconductor giant Advanced Micro Devices were among the biggest advancers in the ETF, up 16% and 14%, respectively.
Nvidia was a standout underperformer, shedding more than 4%.
— Darla Mercado and Gina Francolla
S&P 500 energy was the only sector seeing losses in afternoon trading on Monday.
The group was last down 0.3%, adding to its one-week loss of more than 8%.
The remaining 10 S&P 500 sectors were in the green, led by industrials with a 4.2% gain. Consumer discretionary and information technology weren't too far behind, up 3.7% and 3%, respectively.
The S&P 500 was higher by more than 2% in afternoon trading Monday.
The move put the broad market index on pace for its best day since April 8, when it gained 2.51%.
— Nick Wells and Sean Conlon
General Motors' move to the Nasdaq on Nov. 17, and its possible inclusion in the Nasdaq-100 index as early as December, could bring increased investor visibility and focus to the overlooked automaker, according to Citi analyst Michael Ward.
If GM joins the Nasdaq-100 index it "would have a 0.2% weighting in the Index which represents about $4.6 billion of buying, or 10% of the non-indexed market cap," he wrote.
Additionally, he expects GM to buy back $10 billion in shares by the end of 2027, about 20% of the non-indexed market cap, which will support shares. If it joins, GM will become the cheapest stock in the index with the highest buyback yield, Ward noted.
CNBC recently said GM's switch to the Nasdaq could help it reframe its brand identity and boost its depressed valuation with the exposure to a new set of potential investors. Citi agreed.
"In our view, the structural improvements at GM and the North American industry have been missed, and if GM becomes part of the Nasdaq 100 Index, new investors will need to take a look which could bring added value to the stock," Ward wrote. The move helps reposition GM as a broad technology-first manufacturer, not just a combustion engine maker. "Consumer connection and complex manufacturing expertise position the auto sector to benefit from developing trends in energy storage, autonomous technologies, and connected platforms," wrote Ward.
Citi rates GM a buy with a $131 a share price target, which is more than 50% above Friday's close.
Check out the other names making moves in CNBC's live blog here .
While stocks are bouncing back on Monday after last week's turbulence, they may not be over the hump yet.
"With many investors unwilling to stick their neck out right before year-end, we struggle to find many positive catalysts for stocks over the near-term," said Chris Senyek, the firm's chief investment strategist, in a Monday note.
Seeing downside risks, Senyek added, "We believe markets are likely to remain very news flow driven and need to hold critical technical support levels."
Currently, the S&P 500 is trading just above its 200-day moving average.
Stocks, primarily those exposed to the AI buildout, were hit last week following a bigger-than-expected victory by Democrats in the midterm elections. But Oppenheimer chief investment strategist John Stoltzfus thinks that the market can rebound, as it started on Monday.
"So long as the underlying fundamentals that support economic growth and nurture revenue
and profit growth have not dramatically deteriorated… the market can find opportunity to not just regain lost ground but even rise well above where it had been," Stoltzfus wrote in a Monday note.
This week, he said that all eyes will be on the inflation report set to be delivered Tuesday, particularly off a hot jobs report on Friday, as investors look to predict what the Federal Reserve will do with interest rates at its December meeting. And while some investors were nervous about the AI trade following Democratic victories last week, Stoltzfus doesn't share those concerns.
"It would seem to us that it is much too early to predict the failure of AI to gain traction or achieve profitability," he said.

articles.content_orig:
Lucid Group missed Wall Street's third-quarter expectations as the embattled electric vehicle maker continues an "operational reset" aimed at cutting costs and narrowing losses.
The company on Monday also announced a $1.75 billion increase in a delayed draw term loan from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the company's largest shareholder.
Lucid stock fell roughly 5% in aftermarket trading Monday.
Here's how Lucid performed in the third quarter compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
Despite the top- and bottom-line misses, the company's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of a loss $726 million beat Wall Street's expectations of a loss of $611 million for the third quarter. Its net loss for the quarter was $830.9 million, down from a loss of $978.4 million a year earlier.
Lucid's 2025 third quarter included revenue of $336.6 million, a loss of $3.31 per share and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $717.7 million.
The quarterly results are the first since Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli , who started leading the company in June, announced a restructuring plan that included implementing several cost-cutting efforts and delaying the company's upcoming midsize vehicle from the end of this year until the second half of next.
"Our transformation is beginning to show progress. We are acting with urgency, strengthening the fundamentals and driving greater discipline, while continuing to invest in the priorities to deliver profitable long-term growth," Napoli said in a release.
The company's turnaround plan includes $1.4 billion in cash flow improvements this year as well as focusing attention on a robotaxi program with Uber and Nuro, a factory that's under construction in Saudi Arabia and the midsize vehicle.
Lucid said the capital from PIF is expected to give the company "additional financial flexibility as Lucid delivers on its turnaround program." It is expected to assist in funding "operations and key investments" into the fourth quarter of 2027, including the start of production for the midsize vehicle.
The additional funds boost Lucid's total liquidity to $3.75 billion, up from $2 billion to end the third quarter.
"We are grateful for the continued financial support from our anchor shareholder, which further energizes us to remain focused on execution and on our commitments as we build a stronger, sustainable Lucid," Napoli said.
Lucid said Monday that the company expects to communicate its midterm plan and targets early next year. The EV maker in May suspended its guidance and many targets, citing new leadership and time needed to develop a turnaround plan.

articles.title_orig: Israeli opposition eyes deal with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to oust Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Israeli opposition eyes deal with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to oust Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Avigdor Liberman's 2018 haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription proposal has reemerged as a potential basis for coalition negotiations after the Yisrael Beytenu chairman signaled on Sunday that he was willing to compromise with ultra-Orthodox parties. But how does the proposal compare with the draft legislation promoted by Boaz Bismuth in 2025, and would either framework meet the IDF's growing manpower needs?
The 2018 proposal, developed by the Defense Ministry and the IDF during Liberman's tenure as defense minister, sought to gradually increase haredi enlistment while preserving military service deferrals for yeshiva students. It established annual recruitment targets, financial penalties for institutions that failed to meet them, and a mechanism that could ultimately terminate the special exemption arrangement if recruitment targets were repeatedly missed.
Unlike Bismuth's proposal, which introduced additional personal sanctions against individual yeshiva students, Liberman's framework primarily targeted yeshiva funding and the continued validity of the exemption system itself. It also set a lower exemption age of 24, compared with 26 under Bismuth's proposal.
The differences have taken on renewed political significance as Gadi Eisenkot prepares to receive the mandate to form a government. Liberman's decision to lift his veto on cooperation with haredi parties has opened the door to coalition negotiations, although he maintains that his willingness to compromise does not amount to abandoning his support for universal conscription.
"Willingness to compromise does not mean abandoning values and principles," Liberman wrote in a statement on Sunday, defending his change in political position amid criticism from commentators and journalists.
He emphasized that his 2018 proposal would require adjustments in light of the October 7 attacks and the subsequent increase in the military's manpower requirements.
"It is clear to me that following the events of October 7, the law I proposed in 2018 also requires changes and adjustments, but it still constitutes a suitable basis for reaching agreements," he wrote.
Liberman's 2018 legislation was developed by a committee comprising representatives of the Defense Ministry and the IDF. It passed its first reading in the Knesset in July of that year.
The proposal aimed to increase military enlistment among ultra-Orthodox men without dismantling the existing yeshiva system. It allowed many students to continue deferring their service while establishing gradually increasing recruitment targets.
Bismuth's 2025 proposal similarly preserved the possibility of service deferrals and exemptions but added personal restrictions intended to encourage enlistment.
Neither proposal established an immediate and equal military conscription requirement for all young haredi men.
One of the most significant differences between the proposals concerned the age at which yeshiva students could receive exemptions from military service. Liberman's framework set the exemption age at 24, while Bismuth's proposed legislation raised it to 26.
The enforcement mechanisms also differed substantially.
Under Liberman's framework, annual recruitment targets were accompanied by financial sanctions against yeshivas if those targets were not met.
The proposal's most consequential provision addressed prolonged failures to meet recruitment quotas. If actual enlistment remained below 85% of the annual target for three consecutive years, the amendment to the law would expire after an additional 12 months.
This meant that the special arrangement allowing military service deferrals and exemptions could not continue indefinitely if recruitment targets were repeatedly missed.
However, Liberman's proposal did not establish a new system of personal sanctions against individual yeshiva students who failed to enlist.
Instead, its enforcement mechanisms focused primarily on financial penalties for religious institutions and the continued validity of the exemption system.
The committee that developed the framework also recommended expanding administrative sanctions against deserters and draft evaders.
Bismuth's proposal, by contrast, introduced personal sanctions alongside financial penalties for yeshivas that failed to comply with the law.
Those proposed restrictions included limitations on overseas travel, obtaining a new driver's license before age 23, and eligibility for certain government benefits and economic incentives.
However, the personal sanctions were not all designed to take effect automatically or immediately.
Some depended on the issuance of an enlistment order and the individual's subsequent failure to report for duty. Others were linked to failures to meet broader recruitment targets, while certain restrictions were subject to age limits or delayed implementation dates.
The proposal also included provisions allowing sanctions to be eased or exemptions to be granted under specified circumstances.
For individual yeshiva students, Bismuth's framework was therefore more stringent because it introduced additional personal restrictions.
On the exemption system as a whole, however, Liberman's proposal established a potentially more far-reaching consequence for persistent failures to meet recruitment targets.
Under his framework, the special legislative arrangement could expire following three consecutive years of missed targets, subject to the stipulated 12-month transition period.
Bismuth's proposal included review mechanisms, financial sanctions, and possible adjustments, but did not establish an equivalent automatic mechanism terminating the entire exemption arrangement.
The differences are also evident in the recruitment targets themselves.
Liberman's framework established a target of 3,996 recruits in 2018, gradually increasing to 4,967 in 2021 and 6,208 in 2025.
One version of Bismuth's framework set a target of 8,160 recruits over 18 months, averaging about 5,440 per year.
Under that version, up to 10% of the recruitment target could be met by individuals performing civilian service in security-related fields.
At first glance, Bismuth's initial target appears higher than the target Liberman established for 2018. However, Bismuth's annual average was lower than the target Liberman's proposal established for 2025.
The figures do not represent identical periods or legislative arrangements operating under equivalent timetables.
Several versions of the recruitment targets were presented during the advancement of Bismuth's framework. Each figure must therefore be examined in light of the specific legislative version and period it refers to.
Another significant difference concerns how recruits are counted.
Liberman's framework established targets for national and civilian service separately from military enlistment targets.
Under one version of Bismuth's proposal, civilian service in security-related fields could count toward the overall recruitment quota, up to 10% of the target.
Consequently, meeting the overall quota would not necessarily indicate that an equivalent number of new soldiers had joined the IDF.
The identity of those included in the recruitment figures has also sparked controversy.
One criticism of Bismuth's framework concerned the possibility of counting young men who had already left the haredi community.
If a young man raised in the ultra-Orthodox community but no longer studying at a yeshiva is counted as a haredi recruit, meeting the recruitment target does not necessarily demonstrate increased enlistment among students attending active yeshivas.
Beyond these legal and numerical differences lies a fundamental change in Israel's security requirements.
Liberman's proposal was developed in 2018, five years before the October 7 attacks and the war that followed.
Since then, the haredi population has grown, while the IDF's manpower requirements have increased significantly.

articles.title_orig: White House cautiously upbeat about Russia-Ukraine peace talks this week
articles.title_zh: White House cautiously upbeat about Russia-Ukraine peace talks this week
articles.content_orig:
A fresh round of peace talks between the US, Ukraine and Russia are set to begin Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, as the Trump administration renews its drive to end the nearly five-year conflict even after it announced significant concessions to Moscow.
Russia has made clear it wants the negotiations – the first of their kind since February – to be strictly trilateral, though national security advisers from several European nations, as well as officials from NATO and the European Union, are also expected in the UAE capital for separate meetings.
“We are working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine,” US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner said Monday.
US officials on Monday underlined that posture, saying that the upcoming talks are a new starting point in defining an end to the war, including discussions on security guarantees and a “post-war security architecture.”
“We need to come up with a way that, when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war, and we believe that’s what Ukraine wants. We believe that’s what Europe wants and we believe that’s what Russia wants,” one official said.
However, many – particularly in Europe – have cast doubt on Moscow’s intentions. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said Monday she saw little sign that Russia was willing to negotiate in good faith.
Meanwhile, the US official also said that it would be up to Trump to decide whether to offer a US security guarantee as part of peace talks.
The US will be represented by Kushner and Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff, while Ukraine’s foreign intelligence chief and top negotiator Rustem Umerov will lead the Ukrainian delegation, according to the official with knowledge of the talks.
Russia is sending deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin as delegates, according to Russian state news agency TASS, as well as Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and member of general staff Yuri Zhigarlovsky.
Representatives from the E4 group – the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy – as well as officials from NATO and the European Commission will also be in Abu Dhabi, Umerov said Monday. “We will hold separate coordination meetings with our European partners,” Umerov added.
Asked about the presence of European officials in Abu Dhabi, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Europe has its own channels of communication with Kyiv and Washington, while reaffirming that the talks are “a trilateral negotiation – involving Russia and Ukraine – with the United States acting as a mediator.”
Notably, these talks come amid a renewed push by European nations for a more active role in negotiations over Ukraine’s future, and the security of the bloc at large, after Trump touted a new security deal for Ukraine that “might involve all of Europe.”
“The Europeans will be well represented,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told French media Sunday. “In recent weeks, the Europeans have made their voices heard. They have expressed to the American mediator that no discussion affecting the future of the continent can ignore our expectations and demands,” he added.
Europe has long been wary of any US-brokered peace deal negotiated without its involvement, with Umerov saying Monday that Ukraine was “doing everything we can to ensure that Europe is a participant in the diplomatic process.”
While the talks will remain trilateral, Kushner said that he and Witkoff would also meet with European partners to continue the “close consultation and coordination we have undertaken on European security and Ukraine’s postwar future over the past several weeks.”
“Ultimately, achieving a comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them,” Kushner posted on X.
This will be the fourth round of trilateral talks. All have ended without significant breakthrough.
Earlier this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the most recent trilateral talks in Geneva, Switzerland, in February fell short of Ukraine’s goals, saying “sensitive political matters, issues of possible compromises and the necessary meeting of leaders have not yet been sufficiently worked through.”
The US later postponed a round of trilateral talks that were expected to take place in March due to the war in Iran.
Putin is still making maximalist demands previously rejected by Kyiv, including Russian control over Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, a reduction in the size of Ukraine’s military and the abandonment of Kyiv’s ambitions to join NATO.
John Herbst, senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center and a former US ambassador to Ukraine, said any expectations for the Abu Dhabi talks should be “very modest.”

Civilian deaths in Ukraine are at their highest point since the start of the war, with more than 2,700 killed in Russian strikes so far this year, according to ACLED, a global conflict monitor.
And continuing a pattern seen in previous years, Russian drones and missiles are already hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, but harder and earlier than in other winters, analysts say. Russian attacks on the power grid left more than 600,000 people in the Dnipropetrovsk region without electricity overnight into Sunday, Zelensky said, as temperatures plummet and winter draws in.
Over the past few months, Russia has deployed faster, jet-powered Shahed drones, which are harder to shoot down. At the same time, more missiles are slipping through Ukraine’s air defenses as Kyiv grapples with a chronic shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors that are one of the few defensive weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles.

articles.title_orig: Who is Alice Huang, the woman linked to Nvidia’s CEO?
articles.title_zh: Who is Alice Huang, the woman linked to Nvidia’s CEO?
articles.content_orig:
CEO reportedly ‌had close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing
Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”
Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully ‌supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on ​Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full ⁠responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my ​wife. My ​actions hurt her ​and our children. There is no excuse ​for what ‌I did,” ​Huang said ​in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.

Russia could use tri leader summit to nudge China and US closer to its position on Ukraine, experts say. What we know on day 1,718
Beijing has confirmed that it is discussing a historic meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the US president, Donald Trump, and Russia’s Vladimir Putin . Mao Ning, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry, said at a press briefing this week in Beijing that China “is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state”, which could take place on the sidelines of the Apec summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen this month.
Russia would probably use the summit to nudge China and the US closer to Moscow’s positions on Ukraine , said Sun Yun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center. However, Trump has been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Danny Russel, a former senior state department official who served in Barack Obama’s administration and who is now a distinguished fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
Ukraine again came under attack from Russia on Saturday, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeated his calls for allies to supply Kyiv quickly with missiles for the US-made Patriot system to defend Ukrainian cities . Zelenskyy on Friday had warned that the Ukrainian military was bracing for new ⁠strikes ​by Russian forces against important infrastructure. “We ⁠have intelligence at this time that Russia is preparing new strikes on energy, on ⁠bridges across the Dnipro, on civilian infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said ​in his nightly ‌video address. “The ‌air force and the armed forces of Ukraine ‌as a whole are preparing for defence. It will not be easy.”
Kyiv, along with other Ukrainian cities, has been subjected to near-constant attacks for several weeks. A missile attack by Russian forces ⁠early on Saturday damaged a residential ⁠building in the Ukrainian capital , according to Mayor ​Vitali ‌Klitschko. The city’s military administration, also writing on Telegram, said two people were injured and a building housing a kindergarten was ‌damaged. Russian attacks also damaged energy facilities in the Kyiv region affecting operation of heating and water supply systems in the city, while an important bridge was also hit, Klitschko said, adding “the capital’s energy supply is extremely difficult”. Officials continued to warn residents of the potential for more strikes hours ​after the attack.
President Zelenskyy says he wants specific guarantees from western allies on how postwar security support would function when the war with Russia finally ends . Zelenskyy’s comments in an interview aired late Thursday followed two days of discussions among allies in Brussels that focused on postwar security and reconstruction. They also came before planned three-way talks next week in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine, Russia and the United States, the first trilateral peace discussions since February. “What matters is that it’s clear on paper,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Ukraine’s private 1+1 television broadcast late Thursday. “The question isn’t dozens of points, but simply an understanding of the outcome: If Russia starts [attacking] again, what will happen? Who will do what, with what means, and when?”
The Brussels meetings brought together officials from the US, UK, France, Germany and the European Union, along with representatives from the World Bank and the US investment group BlackRock , Ukrainian lead negotiator Rustem Umerov wrote in an online post. “We separately discussed the threats from Russia to Ukraine and all of Europe, as well as joint steps to counter them,” Umerov wrote.

articles.title_zh: FDA orders new warning on GLP-1s over rare eye condition linked to sudden blindness
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Trump says FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO’s relationship with alleged Chinese spy
The Food and Drug Administration said Monday that GLP-1 drugmakers must add a warning label about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness.
The condition, called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, affects the optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye to the brain. When blood flow to the nerve is reduced or blocked, it can cause sudden vision loss. The condition is permanent with no known treatment.
The FDA said “there is a potential increased risk of rare NAION” in people taking GLP-1 drugs.
The agency’s requirement applies to all GLP-1s, including Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly’s Mounjaro and Zepbound, as well as several older GLP-1 diabetes medications.
Spokespeople for both Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly said patient safety is their top priority.
Previous research has found that GLP-1 use may increase the risk of NAION, and Lilly has said it was aware of studies on the potential link.
The FDA said it began looking into a possible link after a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology that found diabetes patients prescribed semaglutide were four times as likely to develop NAION as those not prescribed the drug.
The agency said it reviewed reports of side effects submitted to its adverse event monitoring system and analyzed data from multiple clinical trials. Cases of NAION have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 drugs, the FDA found. However, FDA scientists were not able to identify a mechanism for how the drugs could increase the risk of the eye condition.
Risk factors for NAION can overlap with conditions seen in people taking GLP-1 drugs, including Type 2 diabetes, obesity, sleep apnea and hypertension.
Dr. Manjot Gill, an ophthalmologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, said the FDA’s mandate for a warning label was appropriate.
While it remains unclear whether the drugs cause the eye condition, she said, it’s been well-documented that they may increase the risk.
Even so, there is little cause for immediate anxiety, Gill said,  noting that the condition is extremely rare.
“We don’t want patients to really get overly concerned and anxious and to stop these medications,” Gill said. “It’s fine to issue this warning more so for public awareness so that patients, should they experience any kind of change in vision, that they do actually go and seek the care of an eye provider.”
NAION is the second most common optic nerve disease in the U.S., occurring in up to 10 out of 100,000 people over age 50, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology .
“Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss,” with GLP-1 use, the FDA said in the release.
The drug labels from Novo Nordisk and Lilly also carry other warnings, including for pancreatitis, gallbladder problems and kidney injury.
The labels also carry a black box warning — the FDA’s strongest safety warning — about a possible risk of thyroid tumors.
Berkeley Lovelace Jr. is a health and medical reporter for NBC News. He covers the Food and Drug Administration, with a special focus on Covid vaccines, prescription drug pricing and health care. He previously covered the biotech and pharmaceutical industry with CNBC.

articles.title_orig: China extends pause on rare earth export curbs for two months
articles.title_zh: China extends pause on rare earth export curbs for two months
articles.content_orig:
China on Monday announced it is suspending export controls on some critical minerals for two months, preserving a broader trade deal struck between Washington and Beijing before an expected meeting between presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Asia next week.
The announcement from China's Ministry of Commerce formalises an agreement to extend a bilateral trade truce that was set to expire on Tuesday. The extension runs to January 10, according to the ministry. China's finance ministry also said a 24 per cent tariff on US goods would be suspended for two months, although it will still charge a 10 per cent fee, according to a statement.
A filing from the Office of the US Trade Representative posted in the Federal Register also said it was suspending action from a Section 301 investigation into China 's maritime and logistic sectors. The US is also extending 178 current Section 301 tariff exclusions for Chinese goods, according to a second filing.
Where does Trump's critical minerals strategy go from here?
China announced a package of export controls on seven heavy rare earth elements last April, before expanding that list in October. It had earlier announced export curbs on battery supply chain chokepoints, including cathode materials, cathode precursors and graphite anode materials, widening a trade rift with Washington and stoking fears of a potential global supply chain crisis .
China accounted for 60 per cent of global mined production of magnet rare earths in 2024 and 91 per cent of global refined output, according to the International Energy Agency. It holds an even higher share for permanent magnet production.
The US and China entered into a one-year trade truce last October during their summit in Busan, South Korea, that paused tit-for-tat tariff measures, deferred rare earth curbs and included a pledge from China to resume importing US soybeans.
However, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week urged Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to “fully and immediately” implement its commitments in Busan, while also raising concerns about “recent Chinese actions”, his department said in a statement.
In a separate statement, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said it remained important for China to fully implement its commitments, particularly in relation to agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals.
“There is an effort that has been co-ordinated between Treasury and the White House to track various commitments made by China since they first met in Busan,” said a former senior US official. “It's not just critical minerals; it is purchases of various agricultural products, where they stand on GE engines and Boeing,”
“And I think there are people … inside the US government that believe that China has overpromised and underdelivered, and they are making a consistent case that the issue that Bessent and Greer went out on was on critical minerals.”
Meanwhile, China said it “expressed serious concern” over recent US restrictions after Washington placed sanctions on two Chinese companies over their alleged ties to the Cuban regime's oil shipping networks supporting the Cuban military.
Mr Trump and Mr Xi are expected to hold a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit held in Shenzhen next week. It would be the leaders' third meeting this year.

articles.title_orig: ‘Forever cruise’ ship Odyssey impounded in Singapore, records show
articles.title_zh: ‘Forever cruise’ ship Odyssey impounded in Singapore, records show
articles.content_orig:
The Odyssey, the "forever cruise" left stranded in Southeast Asia after its owner struggled with financial problems , has been held by authorities in Singapore, according to court records obtained by CBS News.
A Singaporean law firm, Helmsman LLC, is listed as the solicitor in the "arrest" of the ship, but it is unclear whom the firm is representing. A source familiar with the matter told CBS News it is likely a fuel supplier.
"The vessel has been placed under arrest pursuant to a court order," Singapore's Maritime and Port Authority said in a statement cited by the French news agency AFP and other outlets on Monday. "The crew onboard are reported to be well, and arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors. There are no passengers on board."
It added that the ship was "anchored in Singapore port waters." AFP described the ship as being "impounded" by Singaporean authorities.
The luxury cruise ship is currently being operated by its lender after its owner, Villa Vie Residences, couldn't keep up with payments.
Villa Vie owes one supplier in the area approximately $500,000, though it's unclear whether that supplier hired the law firm to solicit the arrest.
A ship arrest is a legal process in Singapore in which a vessel can be detained or seized following a legal claim.
The journey of the MV Odyssey luxury cruise ship, launched in October 2024, came to a sudden end last month in Cambodia, where residents on the ship had just hours to disembark.
According to accounts from multiple sources familiar with the final weeks on board, these details included a scramble to find fuel while stuck at a port in Singapore, a rush by the crew to obtain provisions once food shipments had ended, and the temporary detainment of the ship in Hong Kong.
AFP cited Villa Vie Residences as saying "extraordinary increases" in the cost of fuel amid the U.S. war with Iran had driven its monthly fuel expenses from about $1,800 per guest cabin, to as much as $8,000 in some parts of Asia, where many nations rely heavily on imports from the Persian Gulf.
This story published first on CBS News at 6:24 p.m. on Nov. 8, 2026.

articles.title_orig: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
articles.title_zh: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
articles.content_orig:
Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting.
The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real.
Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions” into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI.
Greynoise said that GT10 is also installing the Python3 release on machines that don’t already have it because the package is required to run the hacker’s backdoor, which is tracked under the name TAC Agent. TAC Agent supports a wide range of functions, including shell commands, system reconnaissance, and persistence. OpenSSH has released a fix that prevents attacks from working.
Researchers at security firm watchTowr said Friday that they, too, were seeing exploitation activity, which was related to botnets and cryptocurrency. Security firm Previdian has also reported similar activity . It said its company’s sensors have seen 20 exploitation attempts from 13 unique attacker IP addresses geolocated to nine countries.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158, resides in OpenSSH, when it runs alongside musl, a Linux alternative to the widely used libc code library. Further, OpenSSH must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account access checks. Additionally, SSH configurations must (1) have at least one account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 function and (2) also be set to use passwordless accounts by way of specifying a “*” in the password field in the /etc/shadow file. Passwordless configurations are standard for certain types of accounts.
Exploits are triggered when an attacker enters passwords with more than 256 characters for a passwordless account. This step occurs when the OpenSSH server hashes the supplied password and checks it against the hash stored in /etc/shadow. The oversized password produces an error that causes musl’s password hashing function to return “*”. The attacks exploit the “misinterpretation of whether a string is intended to be a password hash,” Red Hat said .
Despite the multiple conditions necessary, CVE-2026-123158 poses a serious threat to a large base of machines, most notably those running Alpine, a lightweight distribution of Linux. The ease of exploitation allows hackers to direct malicious commands to any of the millions of SSH servers exposed to the Internet and identify potentially vulnerable ones in seconds. Anyone using OpenSSH should install the update promptly. Those using musl should investigate further.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo delivers veiled rebuke of austerity measures in predecessor’s homeland
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo delivers veiled rebuke of austerity measures in predecessor’s homeland
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV called on Argentine President Javier Milei and the country’s political leaders to “safeguard democracy” and demonstrate a “careful use of words” during his first speech in Buenos Aires.
The American pope arrived in Argentina on Sunday, embarking on a trip that his predecessor, the first Argentine pope, was never able to make.
Leo’s highly anticipated papal visit to Argentina began with a private meeting with President Milei shortly after the pope landed. Milei has received strong backing from US President Donald Trump, with whom Leo, first American pontiff, has publicly disagreed, particularly on the treatment of migrants and the war in Iran.
The pope’s visit comes at a time when Milei’s “chainsaw” austerity measures have led to welfare spending cuts. Milei has also equated state-led social justice programs with communism and has also been accused of undermining democracy through attacks on the press and divisive rhetoric. He has also struggled to secure bipartisan agreements.
“Democracy, then, is also a part of Argentina’s heritage that needs to be safeguarded,” the pope said at a meeting with politicians, members of civic society and the diplomatic corps at the Palacio Libertad. “Democracy is also strengthened by the daily conduct of public life: through willingness to listen, through careful use of words, through the patient search for agreement, and through the ability to see those who think differently as fellow citizens with whom we share a common future.”
The Chicago-born pontiff, who recently cast a mail-in ballot during the US mid-term elections, talked about the importance of the “freedom to elect one’s own leaders through the ballot box.” He urged leaders to recognize the limits of their power, and said that democracy is protected by “confidence in the law”, the ability to freely express convictions and for institutions to serve all parties.
“Authority is most authentic when it is exercised as service, when it looks beyond the immediate, and when it uses its power to promote the welfare of all,” the pope said. An eruption of applause from the audience forced him to repeat his next line: “Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them.”
Leo’s November 8-11 trip is the first papal visit to Argentina in almost four decades and it comes with the added dimension that Pope Francis did not make a return trip home during his 12-year-papacy. Millions are expected to attend the various services and events while the pope is in the country.
A mass held Monday drew a crowd of roughly 2.5 million people, according to official estimates, making it the largest event Pope Leo has held in his papacy thus far. It also surpasses the numbers that turned out in the same spot for Pope John Paul II in 1982.
One Argentine woman, Milagros, told CNN that Francis had baptized her before he became pope. She said Leo’s papacy had brought her back into the fold, and she now attends more religious services.
“The pope’s message reached me late, but it reached me,” Milagros said.
After mass, Leo visited with five people who had suffered abuse by Catholic clergy or within church organizations. A Vatican press release said the pope “greeted them together, imparted his blessing upon them, and expressed his gratitude for the meeting and for their witness of faith.”
Francis’ decision not to visit Argentina was something even his closest friends were unable to explain. Some have suggested the late pope’s reluctance to visit was linked to Argentina’s polarized political culture, with Francis wary that his presence in the country could be weaponized.
The Argentine pope had a strong emphasis on the church helping the most marginalized in society. Francis lamented Argentina’s economic decline which he blamed on decades of bad governance. He contrasted the roughly 5% inflation rate he recalled from his youth with the soaring inflation and high poverty rates of recent years.
In his speech, Leo cited Argentina’s “abundance of human resources” but called for its “wealth bear fruit for the benefit of all and warned that corruption undermines trust in institutions.
Before his election as pope in 2013, Francis served as archbishop of Buenos Aires, where he spoke out on social justice and was unafraid to criticize political leaders.
Leo’s visit, the second leg of his 12-day tour of South America, will underline the ways he continues the reforms of his predecessor, but with his own distinctive style.
Pope Leo, in contrast, has made the church’s social teaching and concern for the marginalized a central concern of his papacy. His itinerary in Argentina includes a visit to a federal prison in Buenos Aires and a stop at a care center for people with intellectual and physical disabilities in Claypole which has been affected by the Milei cuts.
During his presidential campaign and in the years leading up to it, Milei repeatedly insulted Francis, calling him an “imbecile” for defending social justice, “the representative of the evil one on earth” and a “sh*t of a pope.” Milei later apologized for these remarks and called Francis “the most important Argentine in history” following the pontiff’s death in April 2025, repeating the compliment in his remarks on Sunday.
Milei and Francis met in the Vatican in February 2024, with the pope joking with the president: “you cut your hair!” — a reference to the unruly hairstyle which earned Milei the nickname “The Wig.” Milei replied that he had “tidied it up.”
Leo and Milei previously met at the Vatican in June 2025. After meeting Milei in the Casa Rosada on his arrival in Buenos Aires, the pope was presented with the keys to the city of the Argentine capital by the mayor, Jorge Macri.
CNN’s Claudia Rebaza contributed to this report.

Anthropic released new versions of its most advanced models on Monday, with the launch of Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users.
Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. As a result, Fable 5.2 is now cheaper than its primary competitor GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels. Faster inference serving is available for double the price.
Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system , long a sticking point for many enterprise clients.
It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR , which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain.
Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.”
Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card .
“Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.”
Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.”
Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question.

articles.title_orig: He fought France's far right for half a century. Now Mélenchon eyes a 2027 runoff with Le Pen
articles.title_zh: He fought France's far right for half a century. Now Mélenchon eyes a 2027 runoff with Le Pen
articles.content_orig:
French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon published his book and manifesto, "L’Avenir en commun" (A Shared Future), on 6 November, the day before a major campaign rally organised by his far-left France Unbowed party near Paris.
Mélenchon is currently polling in second place, with 17.6% of voting intentions ahead of next spring's presidential election. He trails far-right National Rally candidate Marine Le Pen, who is polling at 36%, according to an IFOP poll for broadcaster LCI conducted from 27 to 29 October.
On the question of Europe, the manifesto backs scrapping rules and regulations that do not align with French interests, including those concerning the EU migration pact and European defence.
Mélenchon's party La France insoumise (LFI), known in English as France Unbowed, has also called for reducing France's net contribution to the EU budget by around €9 billion, a proposal reiterated by the party's finance spokesman Eric Coquerel in October.
This eurosceptic stance bears some parallels with that of the National Rally, which has pledged to scrap a number of EU regulations and standards, particularly those tied to the business sector, agriculture, energy and environmental policy.
However, while both parties advocate greater national sovereignty and challenge aspects of European integration, their positions are underpinned by different ideological priorities.
The manifesto gives less prominence to Russia's war against Ukraine than to France's relationship with Israel, accusing the government of allowing "a genocide to be committed" in Gaza and condemning what it describes as "diplomatic double standards".
On Ukraine, the manifesto backs "a diplomatic framework that would make it possible to secure a ceasefire and the withdrawal of Russian troops", as well as a gradual withdrawal from NATO, as part of a broader foreign policy based on military independence and non-alignment.
In terms of domestic policies, the party backs retirement at the age of 60, an increase in the minimum wage, legislation to curb the concentration of media ownership, as well as expanded public services.
France Unbowed also proposes tax increases targeting wealthy individuals and major corporations, alongside the removal of several tax breaks.
The measures are expected to generate an estimated €106.4 billion in additional annual revenue, according to the party's proposed 2027 budget, of which €81.7 billion would finance additional public spending, with the remainder contributing to a reduction in the country's public deficit.
This comes as France faces one of the highest levels of public debt in the eurozone, with its financial situation raising concerns among financial markets and drawing scrutiny from the European Union.
In recent months, Mélenchon's proposal to freeze or effectively cancel part of France's public debt held by the Banque de France, as part of the wider Eurosystem overseen by the European Central Bank, has sparked controversy.
The proposal would require a coordinated decision at European level. Both Banque de France Governor Emmanuel Moulin and ECB President Christine Lagarde have argued that such a move would violate EU treaties, particularly Article 123, which prohibits monetary financing of governments.

articles.title_orig: BLS Will Not Publish 12-Month CPI, Core CPI Figures For October
articles.title_zh: BLS Will Not Publish 12-Month CPI, Core CPI Figures For October
articles.content_orig:
Falling gasoline prices provided some relief to consumers in October, but Federal Reserve officials are increasingly concerned that inflation pressures elsewhere in the economy are proving harder to contain.
Prices at the pump declined by more than 4%, according to the Energy Information Administration, providing a respite from a surge that had added more than a dollar a gallon over the past year.
However, the consumer price index for the month, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics will release Tuesday at 8:30 a.m., is expected to show only a slight let-up.
Meanwhile, Fed officials say they are worried that inflation initially driven higher by President Donald Trump 's tariffs and the Iran war is proving more persistent than expected, with price pressures emerging in sectors beyond those directly affected by the shocks.
At a time when the central bank is increasingly confident about the state of the labor market, concerns over the cost of living are what are top of mind for the Fed.
"We've been moving up to what historically we'd consider full employment, and the big problem has all been on the inflation side. We go around, we talk to people everywhere in this district, all we hear about is affordability on the business side, the cost," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Monday during an event in his home district. "So we've got to come to terms with this cost-side and inflation-side failure."
The CPI reading for all items is expected to show an increase of 0.3%. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, is forecast to increase 0.2%, according to the Dow Jones consensus forecast. While both would be slower than the respective September monthly gains of 0.6% and 0.3%, they still represent further price pressures.
There will be no annual reading for October because of the government shutdown a year ago, which prevented the BLS from collecting some data and compiling a full index level. Because of the data issue, there isn't a comparable figure for the index.
Bank of America, using an assumed baseline interpolating data for the period last year, estimated the annual growth rates at 3.8% for headline and 2.7% for core, both 0.1 percentage point higher than September and well above the Fed's 2% goal.
Goolsbee said the current run on inflation is defying what normally could be expected from supply shocks and tariffs, with the current situation intensified by the hyperscaler build-out related to artificial intelligence.
"It was supposed to have gone away by now, and we're now starting to see the inflation kicking up in areas that probably weren't from oil prices and tariffs, like a bunch of services. Now this stuff with the AI data center build-out is, to my eyes, starting to look more just like old-fashioned demand overheating," he said.
The massive investment in data centers is creating demand for construction workers, electricity and equipment, potentially adding to price pressures even as AI promises longer-term productivity gains, he added.
Though the Fed in October voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in place, markets are pricing in a better than 80% probability that the central bank will raise rates by a quarter percentage point at its next meeting in December, according to CME FedWatch data.
Goolsbee, who doesn't vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee this year but will in 2027, didn't commit to which way he was leaning on additional rate hikes, though he said current conditions could warrant action.
"The conventional wisdom there is: Be aggressive up front, to never let the economy overheat, because once it gets overheated, it's extremely painful to get rid of that kind of overheating," he said. "So I think we've got to watch out in that space."
The CPI release comes with economic growth strong — 3.4% in the third quarter for gross domestic product and tracking at 3.5% for the final three months of the year, according to the Atlanta Fed — and the labor market seemingly in solid shape as well. Nonfarm payrolls expanded by a much better-than-expected 165,000 in October, while the unemployment rate edged lower to 4.1%, though inflation-adjusted wage growth has been negative.
That puts the inflation reading squarely in focus.
Bank of America said it sees tariff impacts fading but that goods prices could be pushed higher because of AI demand. Further, the firm is cautious about "sticky" services prices as well as pressures from health insurance and autos.
The bank has been hawkish in terms of Fed expectations and sees a December hike as likely so long as there isn't an escalated stock market sell-off that might dissuade the central bank.
"This will be the final inflation report before the Fed's December 8-9 meeting. If our forecast is correct, we think it would effectively lock in another 25bp hike, all else equal," BofA economist Stephen Juneau said in a client note. articles.title_orig: France, U.S. Suspect Iran Was Behind Cyberattack on European Fridges
articles.title_zh: France, U.S. Suspect Iran Was Behind Cyberattack on European Fridges
articles.content_orig:
France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month.
Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions.
Iran has yet to respond officially, but some Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless.
The French hacking, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food in France was followed by a similar attack against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
The Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.
If the IRGC carried out the cyber-attacks, it remains unclear whether they were part of Iran's deterrence strategy.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.
Additional reporting by Farshad Bayan, BBC Persian.

articles.title_zh: China’s rare-earth rubber trades at 22,500 yuan a tonne, about 35% above standard rubber
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
China is testing whether a premium rubber can win a place in electric-vehicle tires. Rare-earth cis-butadiene rubber, made with a rare-earth catalyst, now has a Xinjiang plant rated at 100,000 metric tons a year, about 110,000 U.S. tons. It also trades at a higher price than conventional synthetic rubber.
China Rubber Industry Association data published Nov. 2 quoted rare-earth grade ND9106 at 22,500 yuan (about US$3,400) per metric ton during Oct. 26 to Nov. 1. Conventional BR9000 in Shandong province was quoted at 16,660 yuan per metric ton, so the rare-earth grade carried a premium of about 35%.
For tire makers, the rubber offers better wear resistance, greater strength and lower rolling resistance, and wider domestic production could make it more widely available.
A production unit at Dushanzi Petrochemical Company in Karamay, Xinjiang, completed a successful trial run on June 27, producing premium-grade rare-earth cis-butadiene rubber. The Chinese Academy of Sciences' Changchun Institute of Applied Chemistry announced the result on July 16.
The institute called the achievement a "major breakthrough" and said the core technologies are "fully under domestic control." It said the project would help meet "urgent demand for high-end grades ," support the petrochemical new-materials industry and help "safeguard supply-chain security."
The process makes two national-standard grades, BR1240 and BR1260, which differ in Mooney viscosity, a standard measure of rubber viscosity and processability. The rubber is made by polymerizing butadiene with a rare-earth catalyst, which helps control the polymer's molecular structure and, in turn, its mechanical properties.
Electric cars tend to be heavier than comparable gasoline vehicles and deliver high torque during acceleration, which places greater demands on tire durability. Low rolling resistance reduces the energy lost as tires deform and roll, while wear and fatigue resistance can extend tire life under repeated stress.
Heavy-duty vehicles also benefit from rubber that can withstand high loads, repeated deformation and heat build-up. Greater resistance to tearing and fatigue can improve durability under demanding conditions.
The institute says the rare-earth version beats conventional nickel-based butadiene rubber on wear resistance, strength, fatigue and tear resistance, low-temperature performance, heat build-up and rolling resistance .
The same properties could matter for military tires and other high-performance rubber parts, though the institute has disclosed nothing about supplying weapons or military vehicles.
The industrial result builds on more than six decades of work at the institute. In 1964, scientists Ouyang Jun and Shen Zhiquan published a paper on rare-earth compounds as catalysts for stereospecific polymerization. The institute describes it as the first international publication on using rare-earth catalysts to produce butadiene rubber.
Work on stereospecific polymerization catalyzed by rare-earth complexes won second prize in China's National Natural Science Award in 1982. Researchers including Bi Jifu, Jiang Liansheng and Zhang Xuequan later ran thousands of scale-up experiments and dozens of pilot trials to develop an industrial process.
A second-generation process led by Bi adds automation and domestically developed technology and equipment. His team tackled precise control of catalyst structure, catalyst preparation, tolerance of different feedstocks, and the integration of long-chain branching and functionalization.
The institute says its work progressed from meeting urgent needs of the national economy to supporting national defense modernization. Earlier defense-related work included liquid polysulfide rubber used as a binder for composite solid propellants, which supported China's "two bombs, one satellite" program.

Micron makes memory chips, but the AI build-out has soaked up all available production capacity. articles.content_orig:
Tom Boggioni is a writer, born, raised and living in San Diego — where he attended San Diego State University. Prior to writing for Raw Story, he wrote for FireDogLake, blogged as TBogg, and worked in banking, marketing and construction.
Democrats want answers from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh , demanding to know whether he is hiding secret conversations with Donald Trump .
The president says he and Warsh have talked. Warsh’s official records say they haven’t. And the Fed chair isn’t explaining the gap, the Washington Post reported.
On Friday, the Fed released Warsh’s September calendar, and once again, Trump’s name doesn’t appear. That makes "five months in a row," every month since Warsh took over in May, with no logged contact with the president. It comes despite a request this summer from Senate Democrats that he include any such conversations.
According to the Post, " The calendars are one of the few windows into how often a president reaches the official who leads the central bank’s decisions on interest rates , and previous Fed chairs have recorded interactions with presidents there. The Fed is designed to operate independently of the White House , setting rates based on its own best assessment of the economy rather than short-term political pressure."
On Sept. 16, the same day Warsh and his colleagues raised rates a quarter point against Trump’s wishes, the president told reporters he had weighed in on Warsh’s vote.
“I talked to Kevin, and I said, ‘You might as well vote with the board ’cause it’s not gonna matter,’” Trump said, noting that Warsh lacked the votes to change the outcome.
When a reporter asked if he had tried to sway Warsh, Trump said he hadn’t. “No, I didn’t convince him. No, I said, ‘Do what you want,’” he said, adding that he wanted Warsh “to be independent.”
Neither side has cleared it up, the report notes. The White House has refused to say when that conversation took place, and Warsh won’t confirm it ever happened.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) and three other Democratic senators wrote to Warsh in August, asking him to state in writing whether he had spoken with Trump and to correct his calendars if so. Van Hollen’s office told the Post on Friday that Warsh never replied.
“It’s clear neither Warsh nor Trump give a damn about transparency to the American people,” Van Hollen said. “Under a Democratic majority in Congress, we will continue pushing for that much-needed transparency.”
