Asian and European markets follow US tech rout with many analysts predicting more waves of selling to come
European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier.
A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March.
The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading. But by the close of the day it had clawed back some of its losses to be down 1%, helped by a rise in US stocks when Wall Street reopened.
Germany’s Dax index fell by 2%, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 0.8% and Spain’s Ibex lost 0.6%.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe .
“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”
However, there were signs of easing jitters on Wall Street on Friday, where tech stocks rose, lifting the S&P 500 share index by 0.3% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq closed up 1% – which only recovered a portion of their previous day’s losses.
That followed a stronger-than-expected employment report that showed the US economy added 165,000 new jobs in October, pulling the unemployment rate down to 4.1%.
On Thursday, the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.
Chip stocks led the slump on Thursday, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by more than 60% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 6.5%.
“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.
“[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s [Thursday’s] brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come.
after newsletter promotion
“Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”
However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year. The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 6.35% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 7.5% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”.
He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.”
Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper poised for its biggest weekly fall since March.
Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week.
Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI’s Dots or Meta’s Muse. While Federighi has delivered a functional version of Siri AI on an incredibly short timeline, the company has no illusions that it’s keeping pace with its rivals.
Two significant improvements are expected to be made to Siri in the coming months. One will give the assistant fine-grained control over Apple’s first-party apps, allowing it to do things like rotate and crop images in Photos and organize Safari tabs. Those capabilities are expected to land with iOS 27.3. The bigger change, integration with third-party apps, is likely to land later, in the Spring, according to Gurman. That would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable, for example.
But that’s just the start. Apple is expected to push Siri to become more agentic and enable features that will allow it to perform ongoing tasks, not just one-offs. Gurman says:
Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.

[DAMASCUS] The Syrian Electricity Company signed an agreement with Chinese company Wasion Group Limited on Sunday to supply 6.5 million prepaid smart electricity meters, as part of efforts to modernize electricity consumption monitoring and improve power grid management in Syria. The deal raises questions about its cost, financing arrangements, and potential impact on consumers’ electricity bills.
The agreement was signed at the Syrian Electricity Company’s headquarters in Damascus, in the presence of representatives from both the Syrian and Chinese sides, as part of a broader government plan to modernize the energy sector and introduce digital systems into electricity services.
The media office of the Syrian Electricity Company, which operates under the Ministry of Energy, told The Media Line that the agreement includes the supply of 6 million single-phase meters, primarily intended for residential properties and small businesses, along with 500,000 three-phase meters, typically used by commercial and industrial facilities requiring greater electrical capacity.
According to the media office, the agreement also includes software systems and technical equipment necessary to operate the meters, allowing for more accurate consumption measurements, improved customer data management, reduced electricity losses, and more efficient network monitoring.
The media office explained that the prepaid metering system requires consumers to purchase electricity credit before using power, rather than paying periodic bills based on consumption recorded after use.
The new system is expected to improve electricity bill collection, reduce errors associated with traditional meter readings, and enable subscribers to monitor their electricity consumption more accurately.

Authorities have also not announced a specific timetable for delivering all the meters covered by the agreement or identified which governorates will be included in the initial phase of implementation.
Khaled Abu Di, director of the General Establishment for Electricity Transmission and Distribution, previously announced that the institution had developed a plan to replace conventional electricity meters with smart meters over approximately three years.
In January 2026, Abu Di revealed that around 1.2 million electricity subscribers in Syria still lacked electricity meters, highlighting the scale of the challenges involved in modernizing metering, billing, and revenue collection systems.
The agreement comes as Syria’s electricity sector continues to face significant challenges following years of war, including damage to power generation facilities and transmission and distribution networks, as well as the need for substantial investment to rehabilitate infrastructure and improve the reliability of electricity supplies.
Although introducing smart meters could improve consumption management and reduce commercial electricity losses, modernizing metering systems does not necessarily mean an increase in electricity generation or an end to power outages. Improving the number of hours electricity is available also requires upgrading power plants, transmission and distribution networks, and securing reliable energy supplies.
The prepaid nature of the new meters raises additional questions about their impact on Syrian households, particularly amid difficult economic conditions and concerns about consumers’ ability to regularly purchase electricity credit.
It also remains unclear whether the government intends to introduce changes to electricity tariffs alongside the new system or will limit the initiative to modernizing metering and payment collection procedures.
The agreement represents another step in economic and technological cooperation between Syria and China, as Damascus seeks to attract foreign companies to participate in rehabilitating public services and infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: As War Roils Energy Markets, China Sees Its Emissions Drop
articles.title_zh: As War Roils Energy Markets, China Sees Its Emissions Drop
articles.content_orig:
Rooftop solar in Chengdu, China. Pexels
China’s carbon dioxide emissions have been flat or falling for more than two years as renewables stunt demand for fossil fuels. But the country just saw its steepest quarterly drop since the Covid pandemic, thanks to energy shocks rippling from the Iran war.
Between July and September, China saw its carbon dioxide emissions fall by 3.1 percent, according to an analysis of official figures and commercial data by Carbon Brief . That is the biggest quarterly decline since the 2022 pandemic lockdowns.
The analysis finds oil use fell by 4 percent, year on year, as Chinese drivers flocked to electric vehicles at a time when the Iran war is driving up the cost of fuel. Electric cars accounted for two in three new passenger vehicles sold in China in September, according to industry data . The uptake of electric cars has helped China ramp down oil imports in the wake of the conflict, analysts find .
Emissions from coal, meanwhile, fell by 3 percent, year on year, as the rapid growth of renewables far outstripped the rise in power demand. China added enough wind, solar, and nuclear generation over the same period to power Germany and more than twice as much as needed to meet China’s growing demand. Emissions from the production of steel and concrete also fell amid the ongoing construction slowdown.
China is continuing to build new coal plants despite the decline in coal generation. As the number of generators grows and the use of coal power declines, the average plant is seeing its running hours drop.
The shift from coal to renewables comes even as large volumes of solar and wind power go unused. China is now generating much more clean electricity than its power grid can handle. In the first six months of this year, China rejected roughly a quarter of its wind and solar output.
Analysts say that China lacks the transmission infrastructure necessary to ferry abundant clean energy from where it is generated to where it is needed. Also at issue is a policy that guarantees the purchase of electricity from newly built coal power plants.

Concurrently, China’s special envoy on Middle East affairs has traveled to Tehran to meet with officials of the Islamic Republic.
Trump told reporters he expects to meet with his Chinese and Russian counterparts on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China next week. According to Trump, ending the war with Iran and nuclear disarmament are expected to be among the topics of discussion.
The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Russian President Vladimir Putin was also interested in holding such a summit to discuss peace in Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Zhai Jun, China’s special envoy on Middle East affairs, met with Ali Bagheri Kani, Deputy Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, and Majid Takht-Ravanchi, Deputy Foreign Minister of the Islamic Republic, in Tehran.
This visit comes one week after Ali Bagheri Kani’s trip to Beijing, where he met with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. The concurrent visit of the Sultan of Oman to China has further fueled speculation regarding potential mediation by Beijing between Tehran and Washington.
China’s Foreign Ministry stated that the objective of these meetings is to review bilateral relations and regional developments in the Middle East.
According to a statement from the ministry, Zhai Jun referenced the widening regional conflict, emphasizing that the use of force is not a solution and that the sovereignty and security of nations must be respected.
The Chinese envoy is scheduled to continue his regional tour with visits to Oman and Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Chinese Bag-Maker Songmont Enters Footwear
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Chinese Bag-Maker Songmont Enters Footwear
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Songmont, the Chinese brand that has made global headlines for cultural storytelling that resonates with China ‘s middle class, will launch its first footwear collection Wednesday.
Known for accessories that translate the landscapes, architecture and craft traditions of brand founder Fu Song’s hometown, Shanxi province, the brand is extending its offering beyond bags, ready-to-wear and fragrance with a footwear range inspired by the Wotou shoe.
Wotou is a traditional style named for its resemblance to a dome-shaped steamed corn bun popular in northern China . Traditionally handmade and padded with cotton, the model’s soft construction and distinctive raised seam informed Songmont’s contemporary interpretation for its debut footwear range.
The new silhouette launching this week, retailing for 2,680 renminbi, or $400, echoes the original, while piping joins two leather panels to recreate the ridge across the upper. Songmont’s tiger-tooth hardware adds a modern detail. The toe combines a square shape with softened edges, and layered leather forms a stepped heel inspired by Shanxi architecture. The style will come in 2.5cm and 6cm heel heights.
Songmont said it has spent more than a year developing the shoes, with 20-plus rounds of fittings and refinements. A custom last was designed to accommodate a range of foot shapes, and the use of full-grain cowhide uppers, a double-layer construction, sheepskin lining and high-resilience cotton insoles is meant to balance support, softness and breathability.
The brand added that the footwear launch builds on a design language it has developed across its collections. Its Gather bag, for example, recalls camel bags of the ancient Silk Road, while the Song bucket bag takes cues from traditional kite frameworks.
“As long as we choose things we genuinely like, the brand remains consistent. If we always chase trends or pay too much attention to what’s new, we can end up not knowing what we want,” Fu said about the brand’s approach in an earlier interview with WWD in Paris.
Founded in 2013, Songmont has around 20 stores in China and is expanding at a measured pace, with a focus on customer experience. It plans to open its first Hong Kong store in December, adding a new address as the brand continues to grow beyond mainland China.

articles.title_orig: KFC’s arrival at Italian ski slopes angers food and mountain purists
articles.title_zh: KFC’s arrival at Italian ski slopes angers food and mountain purists
articles.content_orig:
Fast-food outlets at two prestigious Dolomites resorts are Italy’s first, with legal action threatened
Europe live – latest updates
Skiers on the slopes of two of Italy’s most prestigious resorts will be able to dine from buckets of fried chicken between runs this winter as the US fast-food chain KFC prepares to open outlets, infuriating mountain and food purists while prompting a prominent businessman to threaten legal action.
KFC will open its first high-altitude restaurants on the slopes of Cortina d’Ampezzo and Madonna di Campiglio, in the Dolomites, on 5 December, an initiative the company said was aimed at “surprising people” and “reaching places” where nobody would expect to find it.
The move marks a debut for any fast-food outlet on an Italian ski slope, bringing a menu replete with KFC’s most popular products, from spicy wings and burgers to traditional buckets of fried chicken.
The plans appear to have taken people by surprise, not least Alberico Zardini, a majority shareholder in Faloria Spa, the company that manages the infrastructure on Mount Faloria in Cortina d’Ampezzo, where there is to be a KFC at 2,123 metres.
“The mere idea is disgraceful,” Zardini told Il Messaggero . “It’s absurd and shameful to imagine a fast-food joint in the most beautiful spot in Cortina. Do the people of Cortina not realise what we’re risking here?”
Zardini said he had written to the bosses of Faloria warning that he would pursue legal action unless they put the brakes on KFC’s mountain ambitions.
He said it was “a mad decision”, especially because the outlet would be selling fried chicken inside the Faloria mountain club, where a luxury lodge is due to open on an upper floor. “I am 100% against it and will not just sit back and watch,” he said.
The KFC in Madonna di Campiglio, in south-western Trentino on the opposite side of the Dolomites, will be at 1,700 metres on Piana di Nambino, next door to a swish après-ski club.
The two outlets came under the fast food chain’s “quick service restaurants” product range and were the company’s way of targeting a broader market beyond its loyal Gen Z customers, “from young families to mountain lovers”, said Marzia Farè, the chief marketing officer for KFC Italia.
“We strongly wanted this project because it perfectly represents the way we imagine the evolution of KFC: continuing to surprise, reaching places where no one would expect to find us, and doing so without giving up what makes us unique,” she told brandnews.it .
after newsletter promotion
Needless to say, with the cost of ski passes in Italy increasing each year, the outlets will appeal to those looking for cheap food in otherwise extremely pricey resorts.
But Oscar Farinetti, the founder of Eataly, Italy’s high-end food-store chain, has said the brand “doesn’t belong here at all” – while pointing the blame at customers. “We Italian consumers should be a tad more cultured,” he told Il Sole 24 Ore . “We need to acknowledge our assets – our cuisine made of few ingredients and excellent products. There is a lack of studying one’s own roots – we’re eating fried chicken instead of a nice slice of salami with a glass of fresh wine.”
Luigi Casanova from Mountain Wilderness, an NGO that works to protect mountain environments, told Corriere della Sera : “The era of polenta and luganega sausage is over,” while Paola Demagri, from Trentino’s provincial council, spoke about mountain identity being “sold out to Kentucky chicken”.
Others were more measured in their response. Cristian Ferrari, the president of Società Alpinisti Tridentini, the oldest mountain association in the Trentino area, said: “We have nothing against fried chicken, but are we sure this is the issue we should be most worried about?”

articles.title_orig: Birds return to waterfowl park after oil vandalism
articles.title_zh: Birds return to waterfowl park after oil vandalism
articles.content_orig:
Resident birds have returned to Broughshane Waterfowl Park after an oil spill which caused the death of 13 of the flock.
The popular attraction in County Antrim was forced to close after a nearby home heating oil tank was vandalised , causing the oil spill into the pond.
In a post on social media, The Waterfowl Pond confirmed that work is still underway to address the oil contamination and that a number of pens remain out of bounds.
More than 20 birds were transported to the USPCA's headquarters for urgent specialist care following the incident.
The park, which was home to 120 birds, has since reopened.
Broughshane Environment Wildfowl and Wildlife Trust's chairman, Gary Hayward, said about 10-12 birds have returned including two black swans and Nenes.
Hayward said they are back safely in their pens and they are lucky to be healthy.
The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) was first alerted to the incident on Thursday 22 October and have been involved in removing the oil waste.
The agency said the substance involved had been identified as home heating oil or kerosene.
Police said about 44 gallons (200 litres) of oil had leaked from the tank which had been damaged at a business premise in the Main Street area of Broughshane.
Hayward said that there is very little evidence of the oil left as the NIEA have removed the majority of it.
"They have made problems a lot less than they could have been," he told BBC News NI.
He said there is still some oil around the edges, and once the oil leaves the pens the birds will be moved back into them.
The USPCA has also been a key part of the rescue operation.
They said that all of the birds, including geese, ducks and swans, needed bathed and treated due to the level of contamination they suffered.
Unfortunately some had already ingested too much and died as a result.
The Waterfowl Pond offered thanks to the USPCA for looking after the birds.
"We are truly grateful for everything you have done."
It also paid tribute to the support received from the public.
"It's another positive step forward for our park, and we couldn't have got here without you."
Police have said that enquiries into the incident are ongoing and have appealed to anyone with information to come forward.

articles.title_orig: Leaker Envisions a Shorter iPhone With a New iOS Layout
articles.title_zh: Leaker Envisions a Shorter iPhone With a New iOS Layout
articles.content_orig:
A future iPhone could keep its current width while becoming shorter, with iOS preserving room for content by moving some controls into the status bar, in a theory shared by the Weibo leaker known as " Instant Digital ."
Instant Digital imagines Apple shortening a non-folding iPhone once its display has only a single camera cutout or the front-facing camera moves entirely beneath the screen. Taking roughly a status bar's worth of height off the display would bring its aspect ratio from around 19.5:9 to closer to 18:9, apparently making the phone easier to hold and use with one hand.
Controls that currently sit below the status bar could share a row with the time and system indicators. Instant Digital's idea is that combining the two rows would let the shorter display show the same amount of information. The leaker described the layout and proportions as personal speculation.
Apple has already changed how iOS uses the space at the top of the screen with the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo . The ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌'s smaller Dynamic Island supports up to three simultaneous Live Activities, up from two on earlier models. On the ‌iPhone Duo‌, iOS fits a compact status bar into the corner and positions the Dynamic Island vertically along the side of the outer display.
The timing of a cutout-free display on the iPhone remains uncertain. The leaker "Digital Chat Station" has said Apple is testing under-display camera technology and has described an intermediate design  with a visible hole for the front-facing camera, similar to the ‌iPhone Duo‌.
In a follow-up post on Weibo , another user said they expect iPhones to retain a camera cutout and a 19.5:9 aspect ratio in both 2027 and 2028. Instant Digital replied that some sources say the cutout could disappear in 2028. Display analyst Ross Young has separately said he expects the 2028 iPhone Pro models to retain a centered camera cutout.
In a separate post , Instant Digital said they had a growing hunch that iOS would change substantially after the 20th-anniversary iPhone launches in 2027. They expect changes to how users interact with the software as well as how it looks.
Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman reported that the anniversary iPhone will have curved glass and thinner bezels in the biggest overhaul to the Pro line since the iPhone X. Digital Chat Station has also said Apple was testing a roughly 7-inch display for the largest anniversary model with the same aspect ratio as the iPhone 17 Pro Max.
The iPhone X offers a precedent for a hardware redesign changing how people use iOS. When Apple removed the Home button in 2017, iOS 11 introduced swipe-up navigation on the iPhone X.

articles.title_orig: What Hardware Does Your PC Need To Run A Local AI Model?
articles.title_zh: What Hardware Does Your PC Need To Run A Local AI Model?
articles.content_orig:
I've been a staunch proponent of self-hosting AI for a while now, and the points that I usually make are centered around data privacy and the fiscal cost of self-hosting your own models versus paying for a monthly subscription.
One of the most frequent comments I get says that whatever I save by self-hosting my models is offset by my power bill, which always felt hyperbolic. To find out exactly how much local AI inference adds to my power bill each month, I benchmarked a model with llama-bench, the benchmark tool built into llama.cpp, logged power draw with HWiNFO and Nvidia's own nvidia-smi on my RTX 4070 Ti Super PC, and found that the cost is nowhere close to what I'd pay for a single AI subscription. Here is what I found, and how I measured it.
To make the test and an estimation of cost as comprehensive as possible, I picked Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, which is a model that's too big for my RTX 4070 Ti Super's 16GB of GDDR6X memory on its own, and not lacking in capability at any task I throw at it.
At 16.5GB in its UD-IQ4_XS quantization, I tend to offload the experts from eight of its layers to my Ryzen 5 7600X with llama.cpp's --n-cpu-moe flag to get a comfortable inference speed. This also puts the CPU to work on every token generated by the model, so measuring the GPU alone would have concealed a big part of the power bill, which is exactly why I accounted for the CPU in the cost accounting as well.
I used llama-bench , which is a benchmark test that comes baked into llama.cpp (build b11927) to time the two jobs a model does, which is reading prompts and generating tokens. For this test, I gave the model a 2,048 token prompt to read ten times over and instructed it to generate 512 tokens five times over, both starting from an empty context.
While llama-bench ran, I used HWiNFO to log the CPU's package power and nvidia-smi to log the GPU's board power every half a second. Added together, the two peaked at 237.5W while reading and 251.9W while generating.
Then, I took an approach that can be described as hyperbolic in the accounting of costs, which entailed stacking the deck against myself. I priced every token as if my CPU and GPU drew that peak for the entire run, did not subtract their idle draw, and used the U.S. Energy Information Administration's 2026 projected average U.S. residential rate of 18.2 cents per kWh .
The rest of the system, including the RAM, the fans, and power supply losses wasn't logged by HWiNFO, so I'll show what another 100W on top does, which is the figure I would use as the true "worst case."
Cost per million tokens (USD)
To put that in context, or more aptly, in subscription terms, $20 buys about 110 kWh at the currently projected U.S. average rate. At my measured peak of 251.9W, my PC would have to generate tokens non-stop for roughly 436 hours to burn through that, which works out to about 14.5 hours a day, every day, for a month.
Even with the extra 100W on top, it still comes to around 312 hours, or over 10 hours a day. That's counting generation alone, which is the expensive half of the process, since reading a prompt costs well under a cent per million tokens even if you were to consider the worst case.
At this point, you would've likely realized that comparing the cost of running a local model versus paying for a cloud-based subscription service is quite a ridiculous practice. However, there's one final bit of accounting left, and that's comparing the two.
When you pay for a monthly subscription service, the price of each token remains hidden, but the API rate cards from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI don't, which makes them the most fitting standard of measure for what a model's output is worth. I compiled their list prices against my measured numbers for a clear comparison.
Input (per million tokens, USD)
Output (per million tokens, USD)
Output vs Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on RTX 4070 Ti S
67x (Introductory pricing)
There are a lot of misconceptions surrounding the cost of running local models on the hardware you own, particularly relating to power draw. Part of what feeds into these misconceptions is the fact that a GPU running close to its rated power looks and feels energy-intensive, so most people assume that a model keeps the GPU pinned to that figure as long as it's running. However, that is rarely ever the case, because token generation leans on memory more than raw compute.
My RTX 4070 Ti Super peaked at 144W while generating and 177W while reading a prompt against its 285W rating, and even with the CPU's draw and an extra 100W on top, I'd have to keep the model generating continuously for over 10 hours a day before it could match one $20 AI subscription.

articles.title_zh: Rochefort's Kyle Bass on Nvidia probe, China: President Trump is in a 'difficult spot'
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he was ordering the Justice Department to investigate Democratic leaders over what he described as threats against Republican officials, donors and supporters, without identifying the alleged communications or providing evidence of criminal conduct.
"The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States, and others, with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so," Trump said in a Truth Social post .
The alleged threats, the president said, are "extortion at the highest level," he wrote. "I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!"
In his post, Trump claimed that Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan is planning to "go after all young people that believe in Republican Values."
Trump was apparently referencing a speech Slotkin made at a University of Chicago event on Oct. 13. At the time, Slotkin said: "I want young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration?'...I want them to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want. And so let me avoid participating in that.' I want that deterrence message sent."
Slotkin alleges that she, her family and her staff faced physical and legal intimidation after the posting of a November 2025 video in which Slotkin and other Democratic leaders called on the U.S. military to "refuse illegal orders" following the airstrikes targeting boats in the Caribbean.
On Nov. 20, Trump called the video treason and said "an example must be set."
The FBI contacted lawmakers, including Slotkin, days later. In February, Slotkin declined to sit for an interview the Justice Department requested about the video.
"The intimidation is the point, and I'm not gonna go along with that," the senator said in February. A federal grand jury later declined to indict the video participants.
Now, Trump alleges Democrats are threatening legal intimidation against Republican leaders and their supporters.
"Republicans should get smart, fast! Threatening letters have been sent to many people, all innocent, from Democrat Political Leaders," the president wrote.
The White House and Slotkin didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: iPhone 18e Could Feature Bigger Display and Battery
articles.title_zh: iPhone 18e Could Feature Bigger Display and Battery
articles.content_orig:
Apple's standard iPhone 18 and the lower-cost iPhone 18e will both feature 6.3-inch displays and use the same battery, according to the leaker known as " Fixed Focus Digital ."
In a new post on Weibo, the leaker shared an annotated, side-by-side diagram of the phones' purported internals, labeled "Taycan" for the ‌iPhone 18‌ and "Nevera" for the iPhone 18e. Fixed Focus Digital said the diagram was already circulating online and broadly matched what their sources had told them. They pointed to the battery as an example of the interchangeable parts they had previously described.
The diagram's annotations list a 4,430 mAh battery for both models. That would be an increase of about 21% from 3,671 mAh for the standard ‌iPhone 18‌ and about 11% from 4,005 mAh for the iPhone 18e. The notes attribute the extra room in the standard model to changes to the bottom speaker and haptic engine. The diagram also shows two rear cameras on the standard ‌iPhone 18‌, including an Ultra Wide camera, and a single rear camera on the iPhone 18e, just like previous models.
A 6.3-inch display would be a noticeable step up from the 6.1-inch screen on the iPhone 17e . Fellow Weibo leaker "Digital Chat Station" previously claimed the iPhone 18e would retain a 6.12-inch OLED display at 60Hz , along with a single 48-megapixel rear camera and a potential upgrade to the front-facing camera. The same source expects the standard iPhone 18 to retain its 6.3-inch display with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz, along with a larger battery.
In an earlier post , Fixed Focus Digital said a new chip was the only iPhone 18e upgrade they could confirm at the time and suggested the two models would share some manufacturing processes.
Digital Chat Station expects the iPhone 18e to contain Apple's 2nm A20 chip, up from the 3nm A19 in the ‌iPhone 17e‌. Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo has said Apple's lower-end spring 2027 iPhones will pair the A20 chip with 9GB of RAM , up from 8GB. Both models are also rumored to get Apple's C2 modem, which would replace the Snapdragon X80 in the iPhone 17 and the C1X in the ‌iPhone 17e‌.
The iPhone 18e is expected to launch in spring 2027 alongside the standard ‌iPhone 18‌ and second-generation iPhone Air . The ‌iPhone 17e‌ launched at $599 with 256GB of storage , and it is unclear if it will get a price increase like other iPhone models.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia, Palantir, and Tesla Are Sending Shockwaves Through Wall Street With This $53 Billion Warning
articles.content_orig:
For the better part of the last four years, no catalyst has played a bigger role in lifting the broader market than the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) . Whether it's AI-accelerating hardware or AI applications, an IDC report pegs this cumulative addressable opportunity at $22.5 trillion from 2025 to 2031.
Few companies have taken the AI bull by the horns more than Nvidia ( NVDA +2.77% ) , Palantir Technologies ( PLTR +3.48% ) , and Tesla ( TSLA +4.23% ) .
Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) are the infrastructure backbone of AI-accelerated data centers. None of its competitors are particularly close to matching the compute capabilities of its multiple generations of GPUs.
Meanwhile, AI-driven software-as-a-service provider Palantir is a veritable blueprint for deploying AI applications. The company's Gotham platform assists the U.S. military with planning and overseeing missions.
Electric-vehicle maker Tesla is also an AI applications maven. AI is integral to the success of its full self-driving software and its Optimus humanoid robots.
Image source: Getty Images.
While this trio has thrived amid the AI infrastructure build-out, the individuals who know these companies best are sending all the wrong signals to Wall Street .
Though stock market analysts spend day after day studying the same industry and the companies that define it, no one understands Nvidia, Palantir, and Tesla better than their respective insiders.
An " insider " is a high-ranking executive, board member, or beneficial owner of at least 10% of a company's outstanding shares who may possess nonpublic information. Anytime an insider buys or sells their company's stock, they're legally required to file Form 4 with regulators within two business days. This allows investors to track whether a company's insiders have been buying or selling.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/06/26
In the case of this powerhouse AI trio, insiders have been undeniable net sellers of their company's stock over the trailing five years:
Collectively, insiders at these companies have sold more than $52.7 billion more of their own company's stock than they've purchased since early November 2021.
There is, however, an asterisk that should accompany the above data. Since high-ranking executives and board members are often compensated in stock or options , they're required to sell some of their holdings to cover their federal and/or state tax liability. In other words, insider selling isn't automatically a bad thing -- especially if it's for tax purposes.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/06/26
What's equally unnerving, from an investment standpoint, is the relative lack of insider buying . With the exception of one sizable purchase totaling nearly $1 billion by Tesla CEO Elon Musk, insider buying has been practically nonexistent in this trio over the trailing five years:
If insiders aren't buying, historical precedent might explain why.
For more than 30 years, every game-changing innovation has navigated an early-innings bubble-bursting event. This includes the internet, 3D printing, blockchain technology, and the metaverse.
Stock market bubbles throughout history…

AI stocks now ~40% of the market. https://t.co/RxSAh09k6F
The reason these bubbles form and subsequently burst is that investors consistently overestimate the pace of optimization for game-changing technologies . While AI solutions have been welcomed with open arms, we're likely several years away from businesses optimizing these solutions to boost sales and profits. In other words, the door is wide open for a potential AI bubble-bursting event.

articles.content_orig:
By Fred Meintjes 2026-11-09T11:11:00+00:00
Tru-Cape says China’s new tariff deal for Africa is already benefitting South African exporters
The South African fruit business has said that while it has been able to grow exports to China under the country’s zero tariff deal for African countries, there is a short window of opportunity for it to negotiate a permanent trade deal.
The country’s apple exporters revealed this week that they have seen a significant increase in shipments to China.
“The removal of Chinese import tariffs on South African fruit is already delivering results for Tru-Cape Fruit Marketing, with the company’s apple exports to China increasing by almost 50 per cent year-to-date,” stated Tru-Cape Marketing.
”The development has created new opportunities to grow South African apples’ presence in one of the world’s largest consumer markets, while highlighting the need for more competitive market access in India.”
Previously, South African fruit entering China was subject to a 10 per cent import tariff.
The reduction to 0 per cent has levelled the playing field for Southern Hemisphere suppliers, giving South African exporters a more competitive position in the market.
This is likely to also provide further impetus for South African pear, table grape, stonefruit and citrus exporters.
“It is important that we secure a longer-term free trade agreements deal,” the Citrus Growers Association recently commented.
“The playing field is now definitely level, with all Southern Hemisphere countries enjoying a zero tariff,” noted Conrad Fick, marketing director at Tru-Cape.
Tru-Cape currently accounts for more than 20 per cent of South African apple exports to the market.
”South African Royal Gala Red and Royal Beaut apples are performing particularly well, and we are also seeing growing acceptance of the Flash Gala brand, which is helping to increase both volumes and prices,” said Fick.
The country’s stonefruit exporters are also looking forward to their first season in the Chinese market.
“We are particularly excited about building with Sugar Prunes which is already well accepted amongst Chinese consumers,” added Luhan Marais of Icon Fruit.
